title: Lecture 8: Requirements Engineering Fundamentals
summary: This lecture introduces the fundamental concepts and practices of requirements engineering in software development. Students will learn systematic approaches to eliciting, analyzing, documenting, and validating software requirements. The lecture covers the requirements engineering process, various elicitation techniques, the distinction between functional and non-functional requirements, documentation methods including use cases and scenarios, and requirements validation and management strategies.
learningObjectives: Understand the requirements engineering process and its role in software development lifecycle
Apply various requirements elicitation techniques to gather stakeholder needs effectively
Distinguish between functional and non-functional requirements and categorize them appropriately
Document requirements using industry-standard techniques including use cases and scenarios
Validate requirements for completeness, consistency, and feasibility
Manage requirements changes throughout the software development process

sections.title: Introduction to Requirements Engineering
learningGoals: Define requirements engineering and its importance in software projects
Understand the consequences of poor requirements engineering
Recognize requirements engineering as a systematic process

subsections.title: What is Requirements Engineering?
keyPoints: Definition: Systematic process of defining, documenting, and maintaining software requirements
Bridge between stakeholder needs and system implementation
Critical success factor: 60-70% of software failures trace to requirements issues
Involves multiple stakeholders with different perspectives and needs
examples: Case study: Therac-25 radiation therapy machine failures due to incomplete safety requirements
Denver International Airport baggage system failure ($560M loss) due to unclear requirements
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Flow diagram showing stakeholders → requirements engineering → system specification → implementation

subsections.title: The Requirements Engineering Process
keyPoints: Iterative process with four main activities: elicitation, analysis, specification, validation
Continuous requirements management throughout project lifecycle
Feedback loops between all activities
Integration with agile and traditional development methodologies
examples: Waterfall approach: Sequential requirements phase before design
Agile approach: Continuous requirements refinement through user stories and sprints
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Circular process diagram showing elicitation → analysis → specification → validation → management with feedback arrows

exercises: Identify three software systems you use daily and discuss what happens when their requirements are unclear
Map the requirements engineering activities to phases in both waterfall and agile methodologies

sections.title: Requirements Elicitation Techniques
learningGoals: Master various techniques for gathering requirements from stakeholders
Select appropriate elicitation techniques for different project contexts
Recognize challenges in requirements elicitation and strategies to overcome them

subsections.title: Stakeholder Interviews and Workshops
keyPoints: Structured vs. unstructured interviews: when to use each approach
Open-ended questions to discover unstated needs
Workshop facilitation techniques for group elicitation
Active listening and probing techniques to uncover hidden requirements
examples: Interview script for e-commerce system: 'Describe your current order processing workflow'
Requirements workshop agenda for hospital management system with doctors, nurses, and administrators
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Table comparing structured vs. unstructured interview approaches with pros/cons

subsections.title: Observation and Ethnographic Studies
keyPoints: Observing users in their natural work environment
Discovering tacit knowledge and workarounds
Protocol analysis: think-aloud techniques
Contextual inquiry: combining observation with interviews
examples: Observing warehouse workers to understand inventory management system requirements
Shadowing customer service representatives to identify CRM system needs
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Illustration of ethnographic study setup showing observer, user, and work environment

subsections.title: Prototyping and Document Analysis
keyPoints: Throwaway vs. evolutionary prototypes for requirements discovery
Paper prototypes, wireframes, and interactive mockups
Analyzing existing documentation: business processes, legacy systems, regulations
Reverse engineering existing systems to understand current requirements
examples: Low-fidelity paper prototype for mobile banking app to elicit UI requirements
Analyzing GDPR regulations to derive privacy requirements for data management system
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Progression from paper sketch → wireframe → interactive prototype with increasing fidelity

exercises: Design an interview guide with 10 questions for eliciting requirements for a university course registration system
Create a low-fidelity prototype for a task management application and identify 5 requirements it helps clarify

sections.title: Functional vs. Non-Functional Requirements
learningGoals: Distinguish clearly between functional and non-functional requirements
Categorize non-functional requirements using standard taxonomies
Understand the impact of non-functional requirements on system architecture

subsections.title: Functional Requirements
keyPoints: Definition: What the system must do - specific behaviors and functions
Describe system inputs, outputs, and transformations
Typically expressed as 'The system shall...' statements
Directly testable through functional testing
examples: FR-001: The system shall allow users to search products by name, category, or price range
FR-002: The system shall calculate shipping costs based on weight and destination
FR-003: The system shall send email confirmation within 5 minutes of order placement
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Example functional requirements specification table with ID, description, priority, and source columns

subsections.title: Non-Functional Requirements
keyPoints: Definition: How well the system performs its functions - quality attributes
Categories: Performance, Security, Usability, Reliability, Maintainability, Portability
Often have system-wide impact and affect architectural decisions
Can be more challenging to specify and verify than functional requirements
examples: NFR-001 (Performance): System shall respond to user queries within 2 seconds for 95% of requests
NFR-002 (Security): System shall encrypt all sensitive data using AES-256
NFR-003 (Usability): New users shall complete first transaction within 5 minutes without training
NFR-004 (Availability): System shall maintain 99.9% uptime during business hours
subsections.suggestedDiagram: ISO 25010 quality model showing eight quality characteristics and their sub-characteristics

subsections.title: Constraints and Domain Requirements
keyPoints: Constraints: Fixed design decisions and limitations (technology, budget, regulations)
Domain requirements: Requirements from the application domain (e.g., medical, financial)
Distinction from functional/non-functional requirements
Impact on solution space and architectural choices
examples: Constraint: System must be implemented using Java and run on existing Oracle database
Domain requirement: Medical records system must comply with HIPAA regulations
Constraint: Mobile app must support iOS 14+ and Android 10+
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Venn diagram showing relationships between functional, non-functional, constraints, and domain requirements

exercises: Classify 15 given requirements as functional, non-functional, or constraints for an online learning platform
Write 5 functional and 5 non-functional requirements for a smart home automation system

sections.title: Requirements Documentation and Specification
learningGoals: Create well-structured requirements specifications
Apply standard templates and formats for requirements documentation
Write clear, unambiguous, and testable requirements statements

subsections.title: Requirements Specification Documents
keyPoints: IEEE 830 / ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 standard structure for SRS (Software Requirements Specification)
Key sections: Introduction, Overall Description, Specific Requirements, Appendices
Characteristics of good requirements: Clear, Unambiguous, Testable, Consistent, Complete
Levels of detail appropriate for different audiences
examples: SRS outline for e-commerce platform with sections for user management, product catalog, ordering, payment
Comparison of vague requirement 'System should be fast' vs. specific 'System shall load product pages in < 1.5 seconds'
subsections.suggestedDiagram: IEEE 830 SRS document structure template with main sections and subsections

subsections.title: Writing Quality Requirements
keyPoints: Use of modal verbs: 'shall' (mandatory), 'should' (desirable), 'may' (optional)
Avoiding ambiguous terms: 'user-friendly', 'fast', 'reliable' without quantification
Atomic requirements: one requirement per statement
Testability: each requirement must be verifiable
examples: Poor: 'The system should be secure and easy to use'
Good: 'The system shall require authentication using username and password before accessing user data'
Poor: 'The system will handle lots of users'
Good: 'The system shall support 10,000 concurrent users with response time < 3 seconds'
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Checklist for evaluating requirement quality with examples of good vs. poor requirements

exercises: Rewrite 5 poorly-written requirements to meet quality criteria
Create a mini-SRS document (2-3 pages) for a library management system

sections.title: Use Cases and Scenarios
learningGoals: Model functional requirements using use case diagrams and descriptions
Write detailed use case scenarios including main and alternative flows
Understand the relationship between use cases and requirements

subsections.title: Use Case Fundamentals
keyPoints: Definition: Description of system behavior from user perspective to achieve a goal
Components: Actors (users/external systems), Use Cases (goals), Relationships
UML use case diagram notation: actors, use cases, associations, include/extend
Granularity: user-goal level vs. subfunction level use cases
examples: ATM system use cases: Withdraw Cash, Check Balance, Transfer Funds
Actors: Customer, Bank System, Maintenance Staff
Include relationship: 'Withdraw Cash' includes 'Authenticate User'
subsections.suggestedDiagram: UML use case diagram for online shopping system showing customer, admin actors and their use cases

subsections.title: Use Case Descriptions and Scenarios
keyPoints: Structured template: Use Case Name, Actors, Preconditions, Postconditions, Main Flow, Alternative Flows
Main success scenario: step-by-step interaction for normal case
Alternative flows: exceptions, errors, and variations
Scenarios as concrete instances of use cases with specific data
examples: Detailed use case: 'Process Online Order' with steps from cart to payment confirmation
Alternative flow: 'Payment declined' - system notifies user and retains cart
Scenario: John orders 2 books ($45.99) using Visa, ships to home address
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Use case description template with example filled in for 'Book Flight' use case

subsections.title: User Stories in Agile Context
keyPoints: User story format: 'As a [role], I want [feature] so that [benefit]'
INVEST criteria: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable
Acceptance criteria: conditions that must be met for story completion
Relationship to use cases: user stories as lightweight, conversation-focused requirements
examples: User story: 'As a registered user, I want to save items to a wishlist so that I can purchase them later'
Acceptance criteria: User can add/remove items, view wishlist, wishlist persists across sessions
Epic: 'User Account Management' decomposed into stories for registration, login, profile editing
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Comparison table showing use cases vs. user stories with examples and when to use each

exercises: Create a use case diagram with 5-7 use cases for a hospital appointment scheduling system
Write a detailed use case description for 'Register New Patient' including 2 alternative flows
Convert 3 use cases into user stories with acceptance criteria

sections.title: Requirements Validation and Management
learningGoals: Apply validation techniques to ensure requirements quality
Manage requirements changes throughout the project lifecycle
Use requirements traceability to maintain consistency

subsections.title: Requirements Validation Techniques
keyPoints: Reviews and inspections: peer review, walkthroughs, formal inspections
Prototyping validation: stakeholder feedback on mockups and demos
Model validation: checking models for completeness and consistency
Test case generation: deriving tests from requirements to verify testability
examples: Requirements review checklist: completeness, consistency, feasibility, testability
Validation meeting agenda: present requirements, gather feedback, resolve conflicts
Prototype demonstration to validate UI requirements with end users
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Requirements validation process flowchart showing review → feedback → revision cycle

subsections.title: Requirements Management and Traceability
keyPoints: Change management: process for requesting, evaluating, and approving changes
Version control for requirements documents
Traceability: linking requirements to sources, design, code, and tests
Impact analysis: understanding effects of requirement changes
Tools: JIRA, IBM DOORS, Azure DevOps for requirements management
examples: Traceability matrix: mapping requirements to design components and test cases
Change request form: proposed change, rationale, impact assessment, priority
Backward traceability: test case → requirement → stakeholder need
Forward traceability: requirement → design element → code module
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Requirements traceability matrix showing relationships between stakeholder needs, requirements, design, implementation, and tests

subsections.title: Requirements Prioritization
keyPoints: Prioritization techniques: MoSCoW (Must/Should/Could/Won't), Kano model, Value vs. Effort matrix
Stakeholder negotiation when priorities conflict
Release planning based on requirement priorities
Balancing business value, technical risk, and dependencies
examples: MoSCoW analysis for MVP (Minimum Viable Product): Must-have features for first release
Value-Effort matrix: plotting requirements to identify quick wins and low-priority items
Conflicting priorities: Marketing wants feature X, Engineering recommends Y for technical debt
subsections.suggestedDiagram: 2x2 matrix showing Value (high/low) vs. Effort (high/low) with example requirements plotted

exercises: Conduct a requirements review of a provided SRS excerpt and identify 5 issues
Create a traceability matrix for 10 requirements linking them to design components and test cases
Prioritize 15 requirements using MoSCoW method and justify your categorization

sections.title: Summary and Best Practices
learningGoals: Synthesize key concepts from requirements engineering
Recognize common pitfalls and how to avoid them
Connect requirements engineering to overall software engineering process

subsections.title: Requirements Engineering Best Practices
keyPoints: Involve stakeholders early and continuously throughout the process
Use multiple elicitation techniques to triangulate requirements
Document requirements at appropriate level of detail for audience
Validate requirements before committing to design and implementation
Manage requirements as living artifacts that evolve with the project
Maintain traceability to support impact analysis and verification
examples: Success story: Incremental requirements refinement in agile project reduced rework by 40%
Lesson learned: Early prototype validation prevented costly redesign in later phases
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Mind map of requirements engineering best practices organized by process phase

subsections.title: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
keyPoints: Gold plating: adding unnecessary features - mitigate with strict prioritization
Scope creep: uncontrolled requirement additions - enforce change control process
Ambiguous requirements: unclear specifications - use structured templates and reviews
Stakeholder misalignment: conflicting needs - facilitate negotiation and document decisions
Insufficient validation: assuming requirements are correct - implement systematic validation
examples: Scope creep example: Project timeline doubled due to uncontrolled feature additions
Ambiguity cost: 'User-friendly interface' interpreted differently by developers and users
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Table listing pitfalls, their symptoms, and mitigation strategies

subsections.title: Integration with Software Development Lifecycle
keyPoints: Requirements engineering in waterfall: dedicated phase with formal documentation
Requirements engineering in agile: continuous refinement through user stories and sprints
Requirements inform architecture decisions and design patterns
Connection to quality engineering: requirements as basis for test planning
Alignment with module learning outcomes: foundation for applying software engineering techniques
examples: Tracing non-functional requirements to architectural patterns (e.g., performance → caching strategy)
User stories driving sprint planning and acceptance testing in Scrum
subsections.suggestedDiagram: V-model showing requirements phases on left and corresponding validation/testing on right

exercises: Analyze a failed software project case study and identify requirements engineering failures
Design a requirements engineering process for a 6-month agile project with distributed team

assessmentIdeas: Individual assignment: Create a complete SRS document for a medium-sized system (e.g., online food delivery platform) including functional/non-functional requirements, use cases, and traceability matrix
Group project: Conduct requirements elicitation for a real or simulated client, document findings, and present requirements specification
Case study analysis: Evaluate a provided requirements document, identify defects, and propose improvements
Practical exercise: Given a set of stakeholder interviews, extract and categorize requirements, create use case diagram and detailed descriptions
Written examination questions: Distinguish functional vs. non-functional requirements, critique poorly-written requirements, explain validation techniques
Portfolio component: Requirements engineering process plan for a hypothetical project including elicitation strategy, documentation templates, and validation approach
